rationale: The paper reports homogeneous small-molecule palladium-catalyzed Heck reactions and includes author-performed DFT calculations directly addressing olefin insertion/regioselectivity in those reactions. The β-selective Heck arylation of 1,2-dihydronaphthalene is a suitable reaction phenomenon: experimental conditions and selectivity are reported, and the authors computed competing α/β insertion transition states for phenoxide, iodide, and anionic Pd complexes. The public question is framed around explaining/predicting the observed β-selectivity without requiring the solver to reproduce the authors' selected transition states or mechanism.

ABSTRACT: In palladium-catalyzed Heck reactions, partial oxidation of diphosphines often occurs to form diphosphine mono-oxides, which form active Pd species for olefin insertion. It is an overlooked yet kinetically dominant phenomenon under many Heck conditions. Pd(OAc) or in situ-generated palladium(II) salts rapidly convert diphosphines (dippf and QuinoxP* here) to mono-oxides. The weakened P=O donation may remain bound to cationic complex LPd(Ar)<sup>+</sup> or transiently vacate a coordination site to allow olefins to insert on neutral complex LPd(Ar)X. These mechanistic scenarios are observed in the enantioselective Heck

reactions of 1,4-dihydronaphthalene and β-selective arylations of benzofused olefins. These benzofused olefins showed low activity and poor regioselectivity in Heck reactions in previous reports. The partial oxidation of diphosphines is supported by <sup>31</sup>P NMR detection of resting states in catalytic reactions, kinetic profiling using diferent Pd precatalysts, stoichiometric insertion of isolated complexes, and DFT calculations of olefin insertion. Conversely, cationic complex (dippf)Pd(Ar)<sup>+</sup> is an active species for olefin insertion in the α-selective Heck reaction of 1,2-dihydronaphthalene. To ensure good α-selectivity, in situ oxidation of dippf should be suppressed instead. DABCO base is proposed to reversibly bind and stabilize the cationic species. Three Heck protocols deliver arylated tetralin scafolds in high regioselectivity or excellent enantioselectivity, enabling concise syntheses of several natural products and drug motifs.

The density functional calculation was used to determine the equilibrium of phosphine (monoxide)-arm dissociation and olefin binding for oxidative-addition complexes [dippf(O)Pd(Ph)(I)] and [dippf(O)Pd(Ph)(I)]. Geometry optimizations and frequency analyses were carried out with B3LYP-D3/Def2-SVP; single point energies were refined at M06-L/Def2-TZVP with the SMD continuum for diethyl ether at 2 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } . . As expected, olefin displacement of a phosphine of dippf is significantly more endergonic than displacement of a mono-oxide of dippf(O), +15.2 vs +9.2 kcal \mathbf { \hat { m } } \mathbf { o } \mathbf { l } ^ { - 1 } . , consistent with the experimental trend reported by Blackmond and Engle<sup>7</sup> (Figure 13a vs b). Furthermore, the binding of the 1,2-disubstituted olefin is thermodynamically less favored than that of styrene, +9.2 vs +6.8 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup> (Figure 13b vs c).

Next, DFT calculations were performed to identify catalytically competent species and map the energetics of olefin insertion of [dippf(O)Pd(Ph)(OPh)]. Eight ground-state conformers and the corresponding eight transition-state structures for phenyl insertion were located (Figure 14). In every pair of ground states, trans-positioning of the dialkylphosphine and phenyl ligand were disfavored by 11− 15 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup> relative to the cis-isomers, consistent with the strong trans influence exerted by these strong σ-donors.

Rapid interconversion among ground-state conformers being assumed, the regioselectivity of the irreversible aryl insertion is governed by relative free energies of competing transition states of insertion, according to the Curtin−Hammett principle. Accordingly, the lowest-energy ground-state conformer was chosen as the reference for evaluating the activation barriers to \beta \mathrm { - } and α-insertion.

Surprisingly, the lowest-energy transition states for the \alpha \cdot and β-arylation (TS1-α and TS1-β) both adopt transconfigurations (Figure 14a). Their respective Gibbs free energies are 22.7 and 18.4 kcal \mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } . The energy gap of 4.3 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup>, which favors β-insertion, is consistent with >40:1 β-selectivity observed experimentally at 1 0 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } . Both transition structures are stabilized by weak \pi - \pi interaction between the phenoxide and migrating phenyl ring; the displaced stacking is mainly van der Waals interaction or dispersion in nature, according to noncovalent interaction analysis ( \mathrm { N C I } ) . ^ { 4 3 } It is absent in the cis-ground states. TS1-β is further stabilized by a CH-π interaction between the P \mathrm { - } isopropyl fragment and the aromatic ring of dihydronaphthalene, whereas TS1-α is destabilized by close contact of the phosphine and aliphatic fragment of the benzofused olefin.

Natural Population Analysis (NPA)<sup>44</sup> reveals that the phenoxide ligand in transition states TS1-β engenders a significantly higher partial positive charge on the palladium center than iodide (+0.31 e vs +0.04 e). Thus, the electronic efect of phenoxide works in concert with attractive π−π and C−H−π interactions and steric repulsion in two competing transition states, ensuring the high β-selectivity under catalytic conditions using KOPh.

For comparison, the insertion of iodide complex [dippf(O)- Pd(Ph)(I)] was also computed (Figure 14b). Eight groundstate and eight transition-state structures were optimized; the lowest-energy transition states (TS1-α′ and \mathbf { T S 1 } \hat { - } \hat { \pmb { \beta } } ^ { \prime } ) both have cis-configurations, lacking the attractive \pi - \pi interactions with phenoxide. However, the halide complex is unlikely to be the active species for the insertion. Experimentally, stoichiometric insertion of bromide complex D′ gave little Heck isomers (3% yield, 1:1 ratio) without added KOPh.

Moreover, the insertion of anionic complex [ ( \mathrm { P h } ) \mathrm { P d I } _ { 2 } ] ^ { - } was also calculated. Its two lowest TSs for the α- and β-insertions have relative energies of 18.5 and 17.4 kcal \mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } , respectively (Figure 14c). The small energy gap between these TSs is too small to account for >40:1 selectivity in the model reaction. Thus, this anionic pathway was discounted as the major species; it may become a minor pathway in the later stage of the reaction after deactivation of the dippf(O).<sup>45</sup>

scientific_question: For the palladium-catalyzed Heck arylation of 1,2-dihydronaphthalene with 4-tert-butylphenyl iodide under homogeneous solution conditions, what factors control the observed preference for β-arylation over α-arylation, and how do the relative barriers for competing insertion pathways compare under a clearly defined computational model?
computation_relevance: The authors performed DFT calculations on olefin insertion into Pd-aryl complexes relevant to the β-selective Heck arylation of 1,2-dihydronaphthalene. They computed ligand-displacement energetics and competing α/β insertion transition states for phenoxide, iodide, and anionic Pd complexes, and compared those computed energy gaps with the experimentally observed β-selectivity. These results provide private reference values for evaluating a new computational treatment of the same reaction phenomenon.

reference_limitations: The author DFT model uses simplified aryl ligands such as phenyl rather than the full 4-tert-butylphenyl group in the experimental model reaction.
The reported DFT energies are relative Gibbs free energies under a specified continuum-solvent convention; no uncertainty estimates or error bars are reported.
The authors assumed rapid interconversion among ground-state conformers when using the lowest-energy ground-state conformer as the reference for activation barriers.
The computational comparison is intended to rationalize the observed regioselectivity, not to prove that every possible catalytic species or pathway has been exhaustively sampled.
The experimental reaction is conducted at 100 °C, whereas the reported DFT single-point calculations use a 25 °C continuum-solvent convention.
